content: Elevated levels of homocysteine in the blood have been identified as an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease. However, studies conducted in the general population and in individuals with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) have not demonstrated that lowering homocysteine levels reduces the rates of cardiovascular events. Kidney transplant recipients, who often exhibit high homocysteine levels and elevated cardiovascular event rates, differ from the ESKD population in that their homocysteine levels can potentially be normalized through homocysteine-lowering therapies. This raises the possibility that such therapies might benefit this specific group. The objective of this study was to assess the effects of established homocysteine-lowering therapies on cardiovascular mortality in patients with functioning kidney transplants. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Renal Group's Specialised Register was conducted up to March 16, 2015, using relevant search terms. The inclusion criteria required randomized controlled trials that evaluated therapies proven to significantly lower homocysteine levels in individuals with functioning kidney transplants. Studies were included if they compared homocysteine-lowering therapy with either a placebo or standard care, or if they compared higher versus lower doses of such therapies. Two independent authors assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. The results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes or mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes, both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Data were pooled using a random-effects model. The search yielded 359 reports, but only one study met the inclusion criteria and reported relevant clinical outcomes. This study included 4,110 adult participants with functioning kidney transplants and elevated homocysteine levels. Participants were randomized to receive either folic acid combined with high-dose B vitamins or low-dose multivitamins and were followed for an average of four years. While the intervention effectively reduced homocysteine levels (MD -4.40 μmol/L, 95% CI -5.98 to -2.82), there was no evidence that it had any impact on the reported clinical outcomes. These outcomes included cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.20), all-cause mortality (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.22), myocardial infarction (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.35), stroke (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.71), initiation of renal replacement therapy (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.37), and all reported adverse events (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.20). Furthermore, the intervention did not affect the study's primary endpoint, which was a composite of cardiovascular events (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.15). The study was determined to be of high quality. In conclusion, there is currently no evidence to support the use of homocysteine-lowering therapy for the prevention of cardiovascular disease in kidney transplant recipients.
